transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-11-17 15:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Ella Martinez (Horizon - Head of ML), Samir Khan (Horizon - Platform), Priya Desai (Horizon - Security)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and KV/prefix caching recommendations, cost model implications for Horizon's chat+context application. SE demo of console and cost model spreadsheet. Customer wants expected latency at 99p, cost per 1k queries at current prompt sizes, and guidance on Dedicated vs Hosted for PCI-like workloads. Agreed to run a 2-week POC benchmarking run; Redwood to share SOC2 and network diagram.

Topics:
- Current stack & constraints (Kubernetes on GCP, private data controls)
- Throughput/latency targets (200 qps peak, 95ms target 99p for short prompts)
- Caching strategy: prefix vs KV vs per-session
- Batching tradeoffs and autoscaling for Dedicated pools
- Cost model spreadsheet walkthrough
- Security/compliance questions (KMS, audit logs, VPC peering)

Action items (as noted on call):
- Alyssa: pricing + Dedicated SKUs and SLA examples
- Ravi: SOC 2 + network diagram + sample benchmark harness repo link
- Horizon: share canonical prompt set and token distribution by endpoint

Transcript:
[00:00] Alyssa: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Alyssa, AE for Redwood, and Ravi is our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Ella: Hi all, Ella here. Looking forward to the Optimize walkthrough — we've been digging into caching and batching to get costs under control.
[00:14] Samir: Samir from platform. We'll be running the POC if we move forward.
[00:18] Priya: Priya on security. I'll focus on the compliance parts later.
[00:22] Ravi: Great, thanks. We'll start with a short recap of goals then jump into the console and the cost model. If we need to dig into network stuff we'll circle back to Priya.
[00:30] Alyssa: Our high level from marketing was you have a chat+context product, mostly company internal data mixed with user input, around 2 to 6k token contexts, correct?
[00:38] Ella: Yeah that's roughly right. Most calls are 1.5k on average but we have spikes with long histories, so the KV cache idea sounded interesting.
[00:46] Ravi: Cool. For a quick framing: batching reduces per-token overhead but increases latency — depends on your latency SLO. KV/prefix caching helps avoid re-encoding repeated context chunks, big win for multi-turn. We'll show numbers.
[00:56] [01:00] Ravi: (shares screen) Okay — this is Redwood Console Optimize tab. On the left is the suggestion engine — it reads your workload stats and recommends batching window, caching TTL, quant profile.
[01:12] Ella: Is that data coming from a sample ingestion or live?
[01:15] Ravi: Both — you can upload a sample prompt set or connect your route to sample traffic. For the demo I'm using a synthetic Horizon-like set.
[01:22] [02:00] Ravi: Here's the cost model — baseline: no batching, no KV cache. For a 1.5k token median request, a hosted 8xA100-ish profile gives X tokens/sec and cost $Y per 1k queries. If we enable batching with a 20ms window and slab batching to up to 8 requests, you see throughput improve, unit cost drops ~22% but tail latency moves from 80ms to 140ms at 99p in this synthetic test.
[02:30] Samir: That tail jump is the concern. Our product needs 99p under 120ms for short sessions.
[02:34] Ravi: Right — you can alter batching target and instead rely on KV cache for multi-turns. For example, enabling prefix/KV cache with a 30-minute TTL reduces repeated encoding cost significantly — in this demo we see another ~30% cost reduction for multi-turn workflows and keeps short-session 99p latency under 90ms.
[02:48] [03:30] Ella: How is the KV cache invalidation handled? We have dynamic user data that could change.
[03:34] Ravi: Good question. Cache keys are by document hash plus session id; we surface TTL and an explicit invalidation API. You can also tie eviction to your user update webhook. There's a tradeoff — shorter TTL reduces staleness but also reduces hit rate. The console suggests TTL based on observed update frequency.
[03:54] Priya: Are cached tokens stored encrypted at rest? And where is the cache stored in Private deployments?
[03:58] Ravi: Yes, encrypted-at-rest and in transit. On Redwood Private, cache can be colocated in customer VPC with your KMS-backed encryption; in Hosted it's our managed cache with customer-controlled retention and audit logs. We'll share architecture diagrams.
[04:12] [05:00] Ravi: Back to batching: there's also adaptive batching — the runtime will dynamically adjust batch sizes based on instantaneous qps and latency SLOs. So you can set a max batching window and a latency budget per route. In Dedicated you get fine-grained autoscaling policies.
[05:20] Samir: For Dedicated, what's the warmup time for scaling up GPUs? We want to avoid long cold starts during traffic spikes.
[05:24] Alyssa: Dedicated supports reserved pools with predictably available capacity and burst options. Warmup is typically a few minutes; you can provision burst nodes and pre-warm kernels if you know expected spike windows.
[05:36] Ravi: Also worth noting continuous batching and kv cache together: when a prefix is cached you avoid repeated KV reads/copy, so batching mainly groups new contexts and user prompts. That synergy is where most cost wins come from for multi-turn chat.
[05:56] [07:00] Ravi: Here's a concrete sample from the cost spreadsheet (I uploaded it to the shared folder). Baseline cost/1k = $14.8. With KV cache hits at 45% and modest batching we get down to ~$7.9 per 1k. Important caveat: this assumes your model variant and quantization profile; a lower-precision quant gives compute savings but may affect quality.
[07:28] Ella: Do you have recommendations for quantization profiles? We can't degrade hallucination rates beyond current thresholds.
[07:32] Ravi: We recommend testing 4-bit quant for non-critical outputs; for higher-precision responses keep 8-bit. Our Optimize suggests which layers to keep higher precision. We'll run a quality regression eval on your prompt set as part of the POC.
[07:46] [09:00] Samir: About routing — we have EU customers and want region routing. If a prefix is cached in US region, do requests from EU miss?
[09:06] Ravi: Cache is regional by default. For cross-region routing we either replicate cache entries across regions or use traffic-aware routing to hit the right region. Replication adds complexity and some consistency lag. For regulated data you may want to keep cache local to the region.
[09:22] Priya: On compliance, we need SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integration. Also proof of data residency for EU-located customers.
[09:30] Alyssa: We support SSO/SAML, RBAC in the Console, detailed request-level audit logs, and KMS/HSM integrations. For Private deployments, you control the VPC and the cache stays in your environment. We'll attach the SOC2 and data residency docs after this call.
[09:46] [11:00] Ravi: Shifting back to the demo — here's the Optimize rule editor. You can create per-route policies: e.g., route /support/* use KV cache TTL 1h, batching window 10ms, prefer smaller model variant for fallback. You can also attach a quality monitor that runs regression tests on a seed prompt set and triggers rollback if quality drops.
[11:22] Ella: Can we do canary rollouts with different batching configurations? We want to A/B test cost vs latency.
[11:26] Ravi: Yes — console supports canary policy and traffic split by route version. You can run 10% traffic on the batched config and keep 90% on baseline. The console will show cost/latency deltas and flag regressions.
[11:40] [13:00] Ravi: Now a quick look at the profiler traces — here's a 95th/99th breakdown. See how the KV cache hit traces drop the encoding time almost entirely; tails are mostly queuing when we batch aggressively.
[13:18] Samir: Is there a way to pin models per customer for Dedicated so we avoid fallback to a cheaper model?
[13:22] Alyssa: Yes, model pinning is supported — you can pin route to a model version and block automatic fallback for strict SLAs. We can show the rollout policy config later.
[13:34] [15:00] Ravi: Quick note on metrics: Optimize surfaces token-level cost, per-route latency heatmaps, and per-customer unit economics. This is how you can justify Reserved capacity buys internally.
[15:15] Ella: On the cost numbers, curious about edge cases — long context >6k tokens. Do caches still help?
[15:20] Ravi: For very long contexts, prefix caching still helps if there's repeated segments. If entire context is unique each time, caching won't help — you'd look to model architecture (long-context models) and batching. Also consider partial KV caching of the most referenced docs rather than full session history.
[15:40] [17:00] Priya: A few security clarifications: Do audit logs include full user prompts? Can we redact PII before logs are stored?
[17:06] Ravi: Logs can be configured to redact or hash user prompt fields before persisting. For Private, you have full control of retention policies. For Hosted, we can set up PII redaction pipelines; we'll include the config examples.
[17:24] Alyssa: Ok, let's talk next steps — we propose a 2-week POC: Redwood runs a bench with your seed prompt set, we instrument KV cache and batching toggles, and report back with cost/latency/quality tradeoffs. Does that align?
[17:38] Ella: Yes. We'll export token distributions and a seed prompt set today and upload to the shared drive.
[17:44] Samir: We'll also provide a traffic replay harness so you can approximate production spikes.
[17:48] Alyssa: Great — Ravi will send the benchmark harness repo link and SOC2/network diagram. I'll follow up on pricing and Dedicated SKUs.
[17:56] [19:00] Ravi: One more demo note — if you have long-running sessions, consider a hybrid strategy: per-session KV cache plus short TTL for personal data, with a separate doc-cache for static corpora. That gets you most hits without risking staleness.
[19:12] Ella: That hybrid model sounds promising.
[19:16] Priya: And we need to sign an NDA or DPA before sending some of the prompt data.
[19:20] Alyssa: No problem — I'll attach the DPA and Docusign link after the call.
[19:28] [22:00] Ravi: Alright that's the core walk. Any other technical questions?
[22:04] Samir: One: in Dedicated, can we use our own KMS?
[22:08] Ravi: Yes, Dedicated supports customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM in Private or VPC mode.
[22:14] Priya: Two: are there offline audit exports for compliance audits?
[22:18] Alyssa: Yes, you can export logs for offline retention and chain-of-custody.
[22:24] [25:00] Ella: Last quick thing on pricing sensitivity — if we commit to a one-year reserved Dedicated pool, how much lower can the per-token cost go?
[25:12] Alyssa: With annual commit and aggressive batching + KV cache we typically see 30–45% reduction vs hosted pay-as-you-go in our examples. Exact numbers depend on utilization and hit rates. We'll model it in the POC spreadsheet.
[25:30] Ravi: We'll also include a break-even analysis in the spreadsheet that shows utilization thresholds for Dedicated to pay off.
[25:40] [30:00] (brief silence while action items added to shared doc)
[30:20] Samir: Sounds good. We'll aim to upload artifacts by EOD tomorrow.
[30:24] Alyssa: Perfect. Anything else?
[30:28] Priya: Not from security; waiting for the docs.
[30:32] Ella: No, thanks — this was helpful.
[30:36] Alyssa: Great, we'll follow up with the SOC2, network diagram, pricing, and benchmark repo. Thanks everyone.
[30:44] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: some names/acronyms may be slightly off (e.g., KV cache shorthand, model variant names). There were a few crosstalks and brief audio cutouts around 00:50-01:10 and 29:50-30:05.
